messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Taxi/Uber Driver
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 27-year-old African American man who came to treatment after years of trying to stay ahead of reactions he could not fully explain to other people. He works long hours as a taxi and Uber driver, mostly evenings and nights, and described feeling most comfortable when he is moving, watching mirrors, and keeping his attention split between the road, the app, and the people around him. He is single and lives alone. In early sessions, he spoke carefully and without much expression about childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, describing a home where danger often announced itself in small sensory details before anything was said out loud.

What stays with Kwame most vividly is not a single scene as much as a sequence his body still seems to know by heart. As a boy, he would hear footsteps coming up behind him or down the hall and immediately tense, trying to judge from the sound how close the caregiver was and what mood they were in. He remembers the feel of a particular rough fabric against his skin during assaults, and the shock of a specific coldness on his body, the kind of temperature that made him flinch before the blow itself. In telling it, he did not elaborate dramatically; instead he spoke with the certainty of someone whose fear had once depended on noticing these details quickly and accurately. Even now, footsteps behind him can make his shoulders lock and his heart start pounding before he has fully turned around. A rough seat cover, certain upholstery, or a fabric brushing his arm can bring a rush of alarm that feels out of proportion to the present moment. Sudden cold on his skin—from air conditioning blowing directly on him, or stepping out into night air after a heated car—can make him feel as if his body has been pulled backward in time.

As he grew older, Kwame came to believe that something in him had been altered for good. He said more than once that he feels “changed in a bad way,” as if whatever happened then marked him permanently. He does not experience his body as reliable. What troubles him is how quickly it reacts, how it surges into readiness when he knows intellectually that nothing is happening. He has come to see his body as something that betrays him, reacting as if he is still in danger even in ordinary situations. When friends or coworkers have told him to relax or reassured him that he is safe, he has found their words almost meaningless. Safety, to him, does not land as a real condition; it sounds like something other people are able to believe.

These reactions shape his workday in concrete ways. Driving for hire means strangers are constantly entering his space, and he is acutely aware of movement and sound behind him. The moment a passenger approaches the car from the rear or he hears footsteps coming up quickly on the driver’s side, he feels himself go on guard. He watches people in the rearview mirror, scans their hands, and tracks every shift in posture or tone. He chooses routes, neighborhoods, and times of day partly around where he feels he can keep control. If a passenger’s clothing or bag brushes the back of his neck, or cold air from an open window hits his skin unexpectedly, he has to work to keep his face neutral and his driving steady.

Over time, Kwame has organized his life around not getting too close to anyone. He avoids emotional intimacy because closeness feels exposing in a way he cannot tolerate. Relationships have tended to end once someone wants more openness, more consistency, or more physical and emotional closeness than he can manage. He distracts himself constantly—music, podcasts, extra shifts, scrolling on his phone between rides—anything that keeps him from sitting still long enough to feel what comes up. He also uses drugs, describing them less as pleasure than as a way to blunt himself or get through the end of a shift. Alongside this, he acknowledges taking risks that even he recognizes could get him hurt: driving too long, pushing himself when exhausted, sometimes moving through the city with a kind of defiant carelessness. He is highly watchful but also, at times, reckless.

A painful part of his story is how separate he now feels from other people, including from his wider community and culture. He spoke about feeling cut off, as if other people belong somewhere he no longer knows how to enter. Gatherings that might once have offered connection instead leave him feeling apart, tense, and unreachable. By the time he sought help, that isolation had become harder to ignore. What finally brought him in was not one crisis but the accumulation of it all: the strain of spending his workdays on guard, the collapse of another attempted relationship, and the sense that his world was getting smaller even as he kept driving through the whole city. He said he wants help because he is tired of living as if danger is always one step behind him. What frightens him most is that this is simply who he is now; what he hopes, though cautiously, is that he might not always have to feel at war with his own body.
